analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers for carbon emissions and returns most of the money to households as monthly dividends.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2012 by Rep. Jim McDermott with four Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to two House committees and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require coal producers, oil refineries, first sellers of natural gas, and importers of greenhouse gases to buy federal permits for every ton of carbon dioxide their fuels will emit. Permit prices would rise on a published schedule, pushing U.S. emissions down to 20% of 2005 levels by the late 2050s. Seventy-five percent of the money would go back to every lawful U.S. resident as an equal monthly dividend and 25% would go to deficit reduction. A matching fee on carbon-intensive imports (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals and more) would keep foreign producers from undercutting U.S. manufacturers paying the carbon price, with refunds for exporters.
analysis.who_benefits: Every lawful U.S. resident would receive an equal monthly dividend paid from the permit revenue. Because lower-income households spend a smaller share of their budgets on fuel, the flat per-person dividend would more than cover their higher energy costs for most of them, while wealthy households with large energy use would typically pay more in carbon costs than they get back. U.S. manufacturers of steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass, and paper would also benefit from refunds on exports and from the fee on carbon-intensive imports that keeps foreign competitors from skirting the carbon price. The deficit would shrink by the 25% of revenue retained in the Treasury.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All lawful U.S. residents, especially lower-income households

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs 75% of all permit revenue into a trust fund that pays an equal monthly dividend to every lawful resident, with a half-share for up to two dependents.
The remaining 25% of permit revenue is retained in the Treasury for deficit reduction.

The bill imposes an equivalency fee on imports of carbon-intensive goods equal to the cost domestic producers face from the carbon permits, and pays exporters of those goods a refund covering their permit costs, so U.S. manufacturers are not put at a disadvantage against imports.
It sets declining national emissions targets, from 2005 levels through 2015–2019 down to 20% of 2005 levels by 2055–2059, with permit prices adjusted up or down to stay on track.

Permit prices are published five years ahead, with a floor and ceiling set in law (from $6.25–$18.75 per ton in 2015 rising to $93.75–$106.25 by 2022), giving households and businesses a predictable schedule.

analysis.who_pays: Coal producers, oil refinery operators, and first sellers of natural gas would pay for permits on everything they sell or import for combustion, and would face an additional 100% tax on any substance sold without a permit. Those costs would be passed on to consumers in higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. Households and businesses that burn a lot of fuel would pay more than their dividend, and coal-dependent communities and workers would bear the heaviest losses as the price schedule squeezes coal hardest.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and heavy fuel users

drawbacks.text: Fuel costs would rise for everyone. Producers pass permit fees through to consumers, so gasoline, home heating, and electricity would get more expensive, and the price schedule climbs steeply, from $6.25–$18.75 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2015 to $93.75–$106.25 by 2022.

The flat per-person dividend does not fully offset costs for heavy energy users — large homes, long commutes, businesses with big fuel bills — and households in coal-dependent regions would face both higher prices and local job losses as coal demand falls.

The bill hands large discretionary power to the Treasury Secretary, who would set the permit price each year based on how fast emissions need to fall, and to the EPA Administrator, who would define which substances count as greenhouse gases — broad authority with few guardrails beyond the legal price floor and ceiling.
Foreign action is required for the import fee to ever expire, and until then trade partners could challenge the fee as a tariff even though it is designed to match the cost U.S. producers pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is one economists generally rate well: a predictable rising carbon price, full refunds for non-emitting uses and exports, and a border fee that levels the field for domestic manufacturers. The equal per-person dividend means most lower- and middle-income households come out ahead financially even as fuel prices rise; the main real losers are heavy fossil fuel users and coal communities, and the main uncertainty is whether regulators would set prices well enough to hit the emissions targets without overshooting the cost burden.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees the day it was introduced, went to an Energy and Commerce subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott of Washington introduced the Managed Carbon Price Act on August 2, 2012, with Reps. Blumenauer, Stark, Larson, and Rangel joining as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee, with the Speaker to decide which provisions each would consider.
On August 3, 2012, the Energy and Commerce portion was referred to its Subcommittee on Energy and Power; no hearing or markup followed in either committee.
The bill never received a vote in committee or on the House floor and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal producers, oil refineries, and natural gas sellers are better off because the bill died — they avoided paying for the carbon their fuels emit, and no carbon dividend or deficit reduction from permit revenue ever happened. U.S. emissions reduction was left to later, less comprehensive measures.

for.name: Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and designed the carbon-permit-and-dividend structure.

against.name: Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the tax provisions of the bill on August 2, 2012 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report to the floor.

against.name: Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill and sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power on August 3, 2012; it never advanced further.

against.name: John Boehner
against.what_they_did: The House Republican leadership never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the remainder of the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led House never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Coal producers would pay permits on every ton they sell, and the rising price schedule hits coal hardest since it emits the most carbon per unit of energy. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the public's interest in emissions cuts and dividend payments.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and petroleum product sellers
industries.note: Refinery operators would buy permits for every barrel of crude and every petroleum product received, a cost passed to drivers and heating-oil customers. Avoiding the fee was their gain and the public's loss under this bill.

First sellers of natural gas would pay permits on all gas sold, raising heating and power costs. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the emissions targets and dividends the bill promised the public.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass, paper)
industries.note: These manufacturers pay indirectly through higher energy costs, but the bill refunds their export permit costs and imposes a matching fee on carbon-intensive imports, shielding them from foreign competitors that face no carbon price. Their protection from import undercutting runs alongside the public's interest in keeping domestic industry whole while cutting emissions.
